lead: The spark must arrive at a crank angle, so the ECU works in crank degrees. It switches the coil on for a dwell time that stores enough energy, switches it off to fire the plug a set number of degrees before top dead centre (TDC), and retards that angle when the knock sensor hears knock. Spark advance decides torque, fuel economy, emissions and piston survival.
prereq: You need: maps and closed loop from concept of electronic engine control, the load signal from electronic fuel control, and the coil, plug and ignition layouts from Electronic and programmed ignition systems and Distributorless and direct ignition systems.

blocks.text: The coil stores energy only while its primary circuit is switched on. The current rises towards a limit set by the winding resistance and by a current limit in the driver, typically a few amperes. The stored energy is ½LI², where L is the primary inductance in henry and I the current in ampere. Switching off collapses the field, the secondary winding produces the high voltage and the plug arcs.

Dwell time t<sub>d</sub> is how long, in milliseconds, the ECU keeps the primary on before the break. For a given coil it depends mainly on battery voltage: a low battery makes the current rise more slowly, so the ECU lengthens the dwell from a voltage table. This is constant-energy ignition: the same current at every speed.
Dwell angle θ<sub>d</sub> is the same interval in crank degrees. The crank turns N × 360 ÷ 60 000 degrees per millisecond.

blocks.where: θ<sub>d</sub> is the dwell angle in crank degrees; N is engine speed in rpm; t<sub>d</sub> is the dwell time in ms; 0.006 = 360 ÷ 60 000.

blocks.text: At 3000 rpm one millisecond is 18 degrees, so 3.0 ms is 54 degrees. At 6000 rpm the same 3.0 ms is 108 degrees. The dwell time stays fixed while the dwell angle grows with speed, so the ECU starts charging earlier as the engine speeds up. The limit is the gap between sparks of one coil: when a single coil serves four cylinders, sparks are 180 degrees apart, and the dwell plus the spark itself must fit inside that gap. Coil-on-plug systems fire each coil once every 720 degrees and have room to spare.

sections.h3: Spark advance, MBT and the knock limit

blocks.text: The mixture takes a few milliseconds to burn. For best torque the pressure peak should come about 10 to 15 degrees after TDC, so the plug must fire before TDC. Spark advance θ<sub>adv</sub> is the crank angle before TDC (BTDC) at which the plug fires.

More advance starts the burn earlier and moves the pressure peak towards TDC, so torque rises, until a point past which it falls again because the piston works against rising pressure. MBT (minimum advance for best torque) is the smallest advance that gives the maximum torque. More advance only adds NOx and knock.

Knock is the unburnt end gas ahead of the flame igniting by itself, giving a sharp pressure spike that rings the block and, if it lasts, cracks pistons. The knock limit is the most advance the engine tolerates at that speed and load. It falls with low-octane petrol, hot intake air, hot coolant and carbon deposits.

The ECU fires at θ<sub>spark</sub> = min(θ<sub>MBT</sub>, θ<sub>knock</sub> − Δ), all in degrees BTDC, where Δ is a 1 to 3 degree safety margin. At low speed and high load the knock limit usually lies below MBT, so the engine runs retarded and gives up some torque.

sections.h3: The spark map and its corrections

blocks.text: Base advance comes from a two-dimensional map with engine speed on one axis and load (air per cycle, from the air-flow or manifold-pressure sensor) on the other: the same kind of map and interpolation as the fuel table.

items: Light load, 1500 to 2500 rpm: about 30 to 45 degrees BTDC. The charge is thin and burns slowly; knock is unlikely.
Wide-open throttle: about 10 to 20 degrees BTDC. The dense charge burns fast and knocks easily.
Idle: about 5 to 15 degrees BTDC, nudged to hold idle speed.

blocks.text: The map holds steady warm values only. Typical corrections are added to the advance angle:

The sum is clamped to a safe band for that speed and load. Retarding the spark also lowers NOx and raises exhaust temperature, which is how the ECU heats a cold catalyst (see engine fuelling and exhaust emissions).

sections.h3: Closed-loop knock control and misfire detection

blocks.text: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric accelerometer bolted to the block. Knock rings the block at a frequency set by the bore, typically 5 to 15 kHz. The ECU band-pass filters the signal, looks only in a window of crank angle after each spark, and compares the signal with a speed-dependent threshold.

items: Knock seen: retard 2 to 4 degrees at once, for that cylinder only where the ECU knows which cylinder fired.
No knock: creep the advance back slowly, about a degree after a set number of clean firings.
Knock returns: retard again. The timing settles just under the knock limit and hunts there.
Knock persists at the retard limit: enrich the mixture, cut turbo boost, or both.

blocks.text: Fast retard and slow advance keep the loop stable: one heavy knock can damage the piston, while a slow return costs only a little torque for a few seconds.

Misfire shows up as a crank that does not speed up. The crank sensor gives a pulse every few degrees, and the ECU times each segment to find the angular acceleration after each firing. A firing cylinder speeds the crank; a dead one does not. Comparing each cylinder with the average gives a misfire count, which sets a diagnostic code (see On-board diagnostics: OBD-II) and can cut that cylinder's injector to keep raw fuel out of the catalyst.

examples.question: A four-cylinder engine with one coil for all four cylinders needs a 3.0 ms dwell, and the ECU wants the spark at 25 degrees BTDC. (a) At 3000 rpm, find the dwell angle and the crank angle at which charging must start. (b) Repeat at 6000 rpm with the same dwell time. (c) Sparks are 180 degrees apart. Find the time left between the end of one spark event and the next dwell at 6000 rpm if the spark lasts 1.5 ms, and say what happens at 8000 rpm.
steps: (a) 3000 rpm: 0.006 × 3000 = 18 degrees per ms. Dwell angle = 3.0 × 18 = 54 degrees. Charging starts 54 degrees before the spark: 25 + 54 = 79 degrees BTDC.
(b) 6000 rpm: 0.006 × 6000 = 36 degrees per ms. Dwell angle = 3.0 × 36 = 108 degrees. Charging starts at 25 + 108 = 133 degrees BTDC.
(c) The 180-degree gap at 6000 rpm lasts 180 ÷ 36 = 5.0 ms. Dwell 3.0 ms + spark 1.5 ms = 4.5 ms, leaving 0.5 ms spare. It fits.

At 8000 rpm: 0.006 × 8000 = 48 degrees per ms, so the gap is 180 ÷ 48 = 3.75 ms, less than the 4.5 ms needed. The ECU must shorten the dwell (to about 2.25 ms), giving a weaker spark. Wasted-spark and coil-on-plug layouts avoid this by giving each coil a longer gap.
examples.answer: At 3000 rpm the dwell is 54 degrees and charging starts at 79 degrees BTDC; at 6000 rpm it is 108 degrees, starting at 133 degrees BTDC, and dwell plus spark (4.5 ms) fits the 5.0 ms gap. At 8000 rpm the gap is only 3.75 ms, so one coil can no longer give the full dwell.

traps: Adding milliseconds to degrees. Convert first: degrees = 0.006 × N × ms.
Treating dwell angle as constant. In constant-energy ignition the dwell time is held; the angle grows with speed.
Calling advance a time. 25 degrees BTDC is about 1.4 ms at 3000 rpm and 0.7 ms at 6000 rpm.
Saying the ECU always runs at MBT. It runs at min(MBT, knock limit − margin).
Mixing the two loops: knock control changes the spark; misfire detection counts and reports (and may cut fuel), it does not change the advance.

quiz.q: Define dwell time and dwell angle, with units.
quiz.a: Dwell time is how long the coil primary stays switched on before the spark, in ms. Dwell angle is the same interval in crank degrees.

quiz.q: Why does the ECU fire the plug before top dead centre?
quiz.a: The burn takes a few milliseconds. Firing early puts the pressure peak about 10 to 15 degrees after TDC, where it gives the most torque.

quiz.q: Why does the knock limit usually lie below MBT at low speed and high load?
quiz.a: The dense charge is hot and, at low speed, the end gas has a long time before the flame reaches it, so it self-ignites at a smaller advance than the one that gives best torque.

quiz.q: At 2400 rpm the ECU sets a 2.5 ms dwell and 20 degrees BTDC. Find the dwell angle and the angle at which charging starts.
quiz.a: 0.006 × 2400 = 14.4 degrees per ms. Dwell angle = 2.5 × 14.4 = 36 degrees. Charging starts at 20 + 36 = 56 degrees BTDC.

quiz.q: A car knocks on 91-octane petrol but not on 95-octane. What does the ECU do differently, and what happens to fuel economy?
quiz.a: On 91 the knock limit is lower, so the loop holds the spark further below MBT; torque falls, the driver opens the throttle more and fuel use rises. On 95 the limit is above MBT, so the ECU runs at MBT.

quiz.q: How does the ECU detect misfire, and which sensor does it use?
quiz.a: It times each crank segment from the crank position sensor and works out the angular acceleration after each firing. A cylinder that does not speed the crank has misfired; the count is compared with a threshold.

quiz.q: A coil has primary inductance 4 mH and the driver limits the current to 7 A. Find the stored energy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many engines now detect knock cylinder by cylinder, some by sensing ion current across the plug gap. Model-based spark control predicts the knock limit from charge temperature and pressure instead of waiting to hear knock. Search next for "ion current sensing", "constant-energy ignition" and "knock window".

figure.caption: The worked example on a crank-angle scale. The 3.0 ms dwell is 54 degrees at 3000 rpm and 108 degrees at 6000 rpm, both ending at the spark 25 degrees before TDC; the dot is the pressure peak just after TDC. At 6000 rpm the previous spark and the new dwell fit inside the 5.0 ms gap with 0.5 ms spare.
